messages.subject: Two important updates
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph users,

First, I just updated geomorph on Github because there was an issue with plotAllometry - thank Dave Thulman for catching it!

The error was caused by inadvertent out of sequence coding. There was code to alter the model for CAC and Shape-size PCA - which requires a simple linear regression model - in front of, rather than behind the options for PredLine and RegScore, which require the original model input by the user.  This resulted in a model overwrite, rendering any model to have only one slope.  Please be aware of this if using plotAllometry (an update of geomorph from Github will alleviate it).  Also, plotAllometry is a wrapper for the plot.lm.rrpp S3 generic function, which works fine.

Second, last week we sent RRPP version 0.5.2 to CRAN, and it is now active.  Because geomorph depends on RRPP, it would be wise to make sure you are running the most current version.  0.5.2 corrected an issue with GLS parameter calculations in the pairwise function.  Unfortunately, versions 0.5.0 or 0.5.1 will provide results, but they will not be accurate, if using GLS/PGLS.

Sorry for any inconveniences!

Mike

messages.subject: Re: procD.lm() function
messages.body_plain:
Hello Nicole,

The different outputs results from your choice of sum of squares and cross-products (SSCP), SS in short.

SS comes in three types, Type I, Type II, and Type III.

For Type I SS, each term in the model is estimated in light of all terms preceding it (This is why Type I SS is call "sequential" SS ). For size*sex, the effect of size is estimated first. When estimating the effect of sex, the effect of size is taken into consideration. When estimating the effect of the interaction term size:sex, the effect of both size and sex are taken into consideration. For sex*size, the effect of sex is estimated first. When estimating the effect of size, the effect of sex is taken into consideration. When estimating the effect of the interaction term size:sex, the effect of both size and sex are taken into consideration. The procD.lm function defaults to Type I SS. So you observed different main effect of size and sex in mode 1 and model 2. But note that both models yielded the same effect for the interaction term since its effect is estimated in light of the effect of both size and sex in both models.

For Type II SS, a main effect is estimated in light of all other main effects, without regard to the interaction term.

model3 <- procD.lm(coords ~ size*sex, iter = 9999, SS.type = "II", data = gdf)
model4 <- procD.lm(coords ~ sex*size, iter = 9999, SS.type = "II", data = gdf)

In both model3 and model 4, estimates for size, sex, and size:sex will be the same. The effect of size is always estimated in light of the effect of sex, and vice versa. The effect of size:sex is estimated in light of both the effect of size and sex. It is essentially the same as the estimates for the interaction term you obtained in model 1 and model 2.

For Type III SS, the effect of any term is estimated in light of the effect of all other terms.

model5 <- procD.lm(coords ~ size*sex, iter = 9999, SS.type = "III", data = gdf)
model6 <- procD.lm(coords ~ sex*size, iter = 9999, SS.type = "III", data = gdf)

In both model5 and model6, the effect of size is estimated in light of the effect of sex and size:sex. The effect of sex is estimated in light of the effect of size and size:sex. The effect of size:sex is estimated in light of the effect of size and sex. Changing the order of main effect again doesn't affect the estimates for any term.

According to your statement, there seemed to be no particular reason to believe the order of size and sex in the model to be important. Therefore, Type II or III may be more appropriate. The choice between the two depends on whether you would like to account for the effect of interaction term when estimating main effects. If yes, choose Type III; if no, choose Type II.

Regards,
Patrick

> Hello Nicole,
>
> The different outputs results from your choice of sum of squares and cross-products (SSCP), SS in short.
>
> SS comes in three types, Type I, Type II, and Type III.
>
> For Type I SS, each term in the model is estimated in light of all terms preceding it (This is why Type I SS is call "sequential" SS ). For size*sex, the effect of size is estimated first. When estimating the effect of sex, the effect of size is taken into consideration. When estimating the effect of the interaction term size:sex, the effect of both size and sex are taken into consideration. For sex*size, the effect of sex is estimated first. When estimating the effect of size, the effect of sex is taken into consideration. When estimating the effect of the interaction term size:sex, the effect of both size and sex are taken into consideration. The procD.lm function defaults to Type I SS. So you observed different main effect of size and sex in mode 1 and model 2. But note that both models yielded the same effect for the interaction term since its effect is estimated in light of the effect of both size and sex in both models.
>
>
> For Type II SS, a main effect is estimated in light of all other main effects, without regard to the interaction term.
>
> model3 <- procD.lm(coords ~ size*sex, iter = 9999, SS.type = "II", data = gdf)
> model4 <- procD.lm(coords ~ sex*size, iter = 9999, SS.type = "II", data = gdf)
>
> In both model3 and model 4, estimates for size, sex, and size:sex will be the same. The effect of size is always estimated in light of the effect of sex, and vice versa. The effect of size:sex is estimated in light of both the effect of size and sex. It is essentially the same as the estimates for the interaction term you obtained in model 1 and model 2.
>
>
> For Type III SS, the effect of any term is estimated in light of the effect of all other terms.
>
> model5 <- procD.lm(coords ~ size*sex, iter = 9999, SS.type = "III", data = gdf)
> model6 <- procD.lm(coords ~ sex*size, iter = 9999, SS.type = "III", data = gdf)
>
> In both model5 and model6, the effect of size is estimated in light of the effect of sex and size:sex. The effect of sex is estimated in light of the effect of size and size:sex. The effect of size:sex is estimated in light of the effect of size and sex. Changing the order of main effect again doesn't affect the estimates for any term.
>
>
> According to your statement, there seemed to be no particular reason to believe the order of size and sex in the model to be important. Therefore, Type II or III may be more appropriate. The choice between the two depends on whether you would like to account for the effect of interaction term when estimating main effects. If yes, choose Type III; if no, choose Type II.
>
>
> Regards,
> Patrick

messages.subject: Is there any way to manually set the widths of plotRefToFunction images and the size of their landmark points/vector lines?
messages.subject_clean: Is there any way to manually set the widths of plotRefToFunction images and the size of their landmark points/vector lines?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Everyone,

I have a number of outline figures I have created using the plotRefToTarget function in geomorph for publication. However, I have been having difficulty exporting them from R in order to edit them in another program like Adobe Illustrator.

When I try to save the outputs of plotRefToTarget using the default export menu in RStudio, I am unable to save them at a particular size or directly adjust the size of the points produced by the plotRefToTarget images. The closest I have been able to get is saving the outline images as .svg files, opening them in Adobe Illustrator, and then resizing them there to fit the figure appropriately. However, this results in the points of the TPS deformation grids not being the same size on between images on a single figure (i.e., extremes of shape change on PC1) and looks kind of sloppy. Oftentimes vector arrows or points will be very close together and it is difficult to discern points or changes in morphology.

Adjusting the graph size manually using the default plotting function in RStudio does adjust point size, but it is not possible to export the graph at a predetermined width (the width in this function is also in pixels at 72 dpi rather than millimeters, and I am trying to export the image at the appropriate size to make sure the image will be legible in a journal figure). I have tried using the svg() and ggsave() functions to try to save the image in the plots window in RStudio, but they do not appear to work with plotRefToTarget outputs the same way they do with plot() or ggplot() outputs. Trying it produces a blank document.

I have read previous vignettes on how to plot multi-image figures in R with plotRefToTarget (such as https://www.r-bloggers.com/tips-tricks-7-plotting-pca-with-tps-grids/), but this produces the same problem in that it is not possible to control point size or the overall size of the figure. Several specimens are narrow in their x-axis and wide in their y-axis or vice versa, which means the TPS deformation grids have to be manually adjusted or else are too small to be legible. It also doesn't seem to work with ggplot2 graphs.

Does anyone know if there is any way to adjust plotRefToTarget outputs so they are exported at a certain width/size and if there is any way to control at what size the points/vector lines are plotted? I am new to geomorph and R so I am not sure if this is something that can be done with geomorph functions or if it can be done with R more generally.

Apologies if this appeared twice, my computer crashed while I was writing this and I was not sure if it went through.

Sincerely,

Russell

messages.subject: Measurement Error Test
messages.body_plain:
Hello Geomorph community,

I’m attempting to perform a measurement error (ME) test on two fixed landmarks.  I have 10 specimens of differing ages which have been landmarked twice in two separate landmarking sessions.  I’m attempting to compare my session1 landmarks to those of session2.  I believe I’ve coded the measurement error test correctly, but I would greatly appreciate if someone far more knowledgeable than I were to look my code over and let me know if I’ve made a mistake, and which code is correct?  I believe Code 2 is correct, but I’m not sure.

I’ve written two sets of code - I get a 1.99% ME in my first code, and 9.43% ME in my second code.

Code 1:

data <- read.csv("~/Desktop/Error Study/Data.csv", header = T,  sep = ",”)
dat.mat <- as.matrix(data[3:8])

indiv <- as.factor(data[,1])
session <- as.factor(data[,2])

dat.array <- arrayspecs(dat.mat, 2, 3)

GPA <- gpagen(dat.array, PrinAxes = F, print.progress = T)

mod <- summary(aov(GPA$Csize ~ session*indiv))
mod[[1]][2,3]
s2within <- mod[[1]][2,3]
s2among <- (mod[[1]][1,3] - s2within)/2
s2within/(s2within + s2among)

= 1.99% ME

Code 2:

session1 <- as.matrix(data[1:10,3:8])
session2 <- as.matrix(data[11:20,3:8])

S1.array <- arrayspecs(session1, 2, 3)
S2.array <- arrayspecs(session2, 2, 3)

S1.GPA <- gpagen(S1.array, PrinAxes = F, print.progress = T)
S2.GPA <- gpagen(S2.array, PrinAxes = F, print.progress = T)

summary(aov(S1.GPA$Csize ~ S2.GPA$Csize))
mod <- summary(aov(S1.GPA$Csize ~ S2.GPA$Csize))
mod[[1]][2,3]
s2within <- mod[[1]][2,3]
s2among <- (mod[[1]][1,3] - s2within)/2
s2within/(s2within + s2among)

= 9.4% ME

Many thanks,
-----
Sean G .Swaters

MA Student

messages.subject_clean: shape analyses to compare partial fossils to complete modern specimens
messages.body_plain:
Dear Geomorphers (& apologies for the cross-post if you're also on Morphmet),

I'm seeking advice on how to approach a dataset of ~400 microCT scans of fossil frog ilia (hip bones) that are preserved with varying completeness along the ilial shaft, meaning that some are broken off shorter than others.

Otherwise they are fairly simple structures with an elongate tubular shaft that articulates with the sacrum anteriorly, and a partial socket on the other end that articulates with the pubis and ischium posteriorly to hold the femoral head in a ball&socket joint. I include a screenshot here of a surface model of a right ilium in lateral view, segmented from a CT scan of a complete ethanol-preserved frog (left), and 3 fossil ilia (right) it to illustrate the degree of variation in shaft length caused by preservation.

I'm considering a few 3D approaches to analyse the fossils together with whole body scans of modern frogs, and I would appreciate some feedback regarding how to deal with breakage/missing data. These are, but not limited to:

anatomically-defined and sliding semi-landmarks
high density point cloud comparison, or GPSA (Pomidor et al. 2016 <https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0150368>)
pseudolandmarks in auto3dgm (Boyer et al. 2015 <https://anatomypubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ar.23084>)
For extant frogs I prefer to work with the whole skeleton (either in the volume or as a surface mesh), because the ilium is not always possible to cleanly isolate from adjacent bones. Checkpoint Stratovan seems a good solution for landmarking since it can take both formats, but I'm still stuck with the issue of how to compare broken fossils. I've thought of working backwards with the extant specimens - first landmarking the entire structure and then systematically deleting points along the shaft to see if/when the signal is lost. But I'm not sure if one can delete points from patches or curves, if I would use those to describe the shaft. I don't believe that estimating missing landmarks would be appropriate in this case.

Apologies for the long post, but I would really appreciate any ideas on how to proceed.

Best,

Christy

University of Melbourne / Museums Victoria
